prompt: What is a module in Python?
choices: A Python file whose functions and variables can be used by other programs.
A folder that holds all the files for one project.
A function that is defined inside another function.
A block of code that repeats until a condition is False.
explain: Any file ending in .py can be a module, and its name without the .py is the name you import.

prompt: What is the difference between import math and from math import sqrt?
choices: The first form is faster, the second form is slower.
The first form gives you the whole module under the name math, the second gives you the single name sqrt.
The first form only works for built-in modules.
There is no difference apart from how much you type.
explain: With import math you write math.sqrt, and with from math import sqrt you write sqrt on its own.

prompt: What does the keyword as do in the line import numpy as np?
choices: It installs numpy if it is missing.
It imports only part of the numpy module.
It checks that numpy is the right version.
It gives the module a shorter name to use in this file.
explain: An alias is just a nickname, and np for numpy is a convention the whole Python community follows.

code:
def sqrt(n):
    return "my own version"

from math import sqrt

print(sqrt(16))
choices: my own version
It raises an error because sqrt is defined twice
explain: The import comes last here, so the name sqrt ends up pointing at the math version instead of yours.

prompt: In what order does Python search when you write import helpers?
choices: Only the folder your script is in, and nowhere else.
The internet first, then your computer.
Built-in modules first, then the current directory, then the folders in sys.path.
Installed packages first, then built-in modules, then your own files.
explain: The first match found wins, which is why the search order is worth knowing.

prompt: You save your own file called random.py next to your script, then write import random. What happens?
choices: Python imports your file instead of the standard random module.
Python refuses to run and reports a duplicate module name.
Python imports the standard random module and ignores your file.
Python merges the two so both sets of functions are available.
explain: Your own file shadows the standard module, which is why naming a file after a standard module causes confusing bugs.

prompt: Which is the strongest reason to split a long program into modules?
choices: Python programs are limited to a few hundred lines per file.
Code written once in a module can be reused by many programs without copying it.
Modules make a program run noticeably faster.
Only code inside a module can define functions.
explain: Modules exist for reuse and organisation, so a fix made in one place reaches everything that imports it.

prompt: What is __name__ set to inside a file that has been imported by another file?
choices: "__main__", the same as when it is run directly.
The name of the module, which is the filename without .py.
The name of the file that imported it.
It is not set at all until you assign it.
explain: Importing calculator.py sets its __name__ to "calculator", which is what makes the main guard skip.

prompt: Why do people put test code inside if __name__ == "__main__":?
choices: It makes the test code run before anything else in the file.
It is the only way to call a function you have just defined.
It stops the test code from running when the file is imported as a module.
It hides the test code from anyone reading the file.
explain: Without the guard, importing the module would run the tests as a side effect every single time.

prompt: Why would you create a virtual environment for a project?
choices: It makes the project's code run faster.
It keeps the project's packages separate so two projects can use different versions.
It is required before you can import any standard library module.
It compresses the project so it takes up less disk space.
explain: Each environment has its own packages, which is what stops one project's upgrade from breaking another.
